question_text: A ballet dancer spinning with her arms stretched folds her arms. What happens to her angular velocity?

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The law
lines: No external torque acts, so angular
steps.why: Angular momentum stays fixed only while no outside turning force acts, so that condition has to be stated before the equation is used. The dancer's own muscles move mass about, but they apply no torque about the spin axis.
common_mistakes: Explaining with energy. The conserved quantity here is angular momentum.

recall.must_convey: That angular momentum I-omega is conserved since no external torque acts.

steps.memory_tip: No external torque acts, so the PRODUCT Iω is fixed. If I falls, ω must rise.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name the condition — no external torque — before writing I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂.

steps.label: The result
lines: Folding the arms brings mass towards
the axis, so I decreases and
steps.why: Iω cannot change, so if one factor falls the other must rise. Mass brought towards the axis lowers I and raises ω; mass moved away from the axis raises I and lowers ω.
common_mistakes: Saying she spins faster "because she pushes" — no torque is applied; I changed.

recall.must_convey: That folding decreases I so omega increases.

steps.memory_tip: Halving a mass’s distance from the axis quarters its contribution to I. The r is squared.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Both halves of the chain — I decreases, so ω increases.

insider_note: Write I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂ before the answer. The equation is the first mark; increases on its own is only the second.
